PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 93 — Lesson 117: Dizziness, Vertigo & Syncope

FNP-level goal: Replace the vague complaint of dizziness with a time- and trigger-based syndrome, distinguish peripheral vestibular disorders from possible central neurologic disease, and evaluate syncope for cardiac and hemodynamic danger before reassuring the patient.

Learning Objectives

  • Classify dizziness into vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium, and nonspecific lightheadedness using timing, triggers, and associated symptoms.
  • Recognize benign positional vertigo patterns while identifying central-vertigo and posterior-circulation stroke red flags.
  • Perform a safe initial syncope evaluation with history, focused examination, orthostatic vital signs when appropriate, and ECG.
  • Distinguish likely reflex or orthostatic syncope from high-risk cardiac syncope without relying on age or a single normal test alone.
  • Use emergency, urgent outpatient, and routine follow-up dispositions based on physiology, injury, recurrence, comorbidities, and access to care.

Part 1 — Make the Patient’s Word More Precise

Dizziness can mean spinning, faintness, imbalance, weakness, anxiety, blurred vision, or a sense of disconnection. Asking only whether the patient is dizzy produces a low-value differential. Ask the patient to describe what happens without offering the answer: Do you feel motion? Do you feel you will pass out? Do you lose balance while walking? What were you doing when it began? How long does each episode last?

A practical framework has four symptom categories. Vertigo is an illusion of movement. Presyncope is a feeling of impending faint without loss of consciousness. Disequilibrium is unsteadiness, especially while walking. Nonspecific dizziness may be multifactorial and should not be dismissed. Timing, triggers, medications, vital signs, gait, neurologic symptoms, hearing symptoms, and cardiovascular context are more useful than the label alone.

Part 2 — The Time-and-Trigger Approach

Ask whether symptoms are brief and triggered, spontaneous and episodic, or continuous for hours to days. Brief vertigo consistently triggered by rolling in bed, looking up, or turning the head can fit benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). Continuous acute vertigo with nausea, gait difficulty, and nystagmus may reflect a peripheral vestibular syndrome but can also reflect central stroke. Recurrent spontaneous episodes broaden the differential to vestibular migraine, arrhythmia, transient ischemia, panic, metabolic causes, and other disorders.

Triggers are clues, not conclusions. A patient who becomes dizzy when standing may have orthostatic hypotension, volume depletion, medication effect, autonomic dysfunction, anemia, or cardiac disease. Dizziness during exertion, with palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea, or sudden collapse increases concern for a cardiovascular cause.

Part 3 — Peripheral Vertigo Patterns

BPPV usually causes brief, position-triggered spinning without persistent neurologic deficits. Diagnosis and repositioning maneuvers depend on a compatible syndrome and clinician training. Vestibular neuritis can cause an acute continuous vestibular syndrome with prolonged vertigo, nausea, and gait disturbance, typically without focal neurologic deficits. Ménière-type patterns may include episodic vertigo with fluctuating hearing symptoms and aural fullness, but new hearing loss, severe symptoms, or atypical features require broader assessment.

Do not prescribe a vestibular diagnosis because the patient has nausea or nystagmus. Confirm the time course, triggers, neurologic examination, gait, hearing symptoms, and vascular risk. Persistent suppressive medication without a diagnostic and rehabilitation plan can delay recovery and obscure the real syndrome.

Part 4 — Central Vertigo and Posterior Stroke Safety

Posterior-circulation or brainstem stroke may present with vertigo, severe imbalance, double vision, dysarthria, dysphagia, new headache or neck pain, weakness, numbness, altered consciousness, or inability to walk. Some patients do not have the classic unilateral facial droop or arm weakness. Severe gait or truncal instability, focal neurologic signs, direction-changing or otherwise concerning nystagmus, and high vascular-risk context should lower the threshold for emergency stroke-capable evaluation.

The HINTS examination is not a general screening shortcut. It is designed for selected patients with a continuous acute vestibular syndrome and requires training and correct application. It should not be used to reassure a patient with intermittent positional symptoms, no active nystagmus, or an examination outside the clinician’s competence. When concern for central disease remains, the safe action is emergency evaluation rather than overconfidence in a bedside maneuver.

Part 5 — Syncope Is Different From a Fall or Seizure

Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery. A fall without loss of consciousness, seizure, intoxication, hypoglycemia, stroke, psychogenic events, and mechanical collapse may mimic syncope but have different workups. Ask witnesses what happened before, during, and after the event: posture, prodrome, pallor, movements, injury, duration, tongue injury, incontinence, confusion, recovery time, and associated palpitations or chest pain.

Brief myoclonic movements can occur with syncope, so movement alone does not prove seizure. Prolonged post-event confusion, a convincing epileptic pattern, or persistent neurologic deficit requires a different pathway. The objective is to reconstruct physiology, not to choose a label based on one dramatic detail.

Part 6 — Initial Syncope Evaluation

Every true syncope episode deserves a detailed history, focused physical examination, heart rate and blood pressure assessment, and a 12-lead ECG. Orthostatic measurements are useful when orthostasis is plausible and the patient can be assessed safely. Review medications carefully: antihypertensives, diuretics, vasodilators, alpha-blocking agents, sedatives, diabetes therapies, and substances may contribute. Ask about hydration, bleeding, infection, diarrhea, vomiting, heat exposure, and nutritional intake.

Testing beyond this initial evaluation should be targeted. Broad laboratory panels, routine neuroimaging, carotid studies, or echocardiography are not substitutes for clinical reasoning. They may be appropriate when history, examination, ECG, or comorbid disease indicates a specific concern. The question is: what dangerous condition am I evaluating, and will this test change the next step?

Part 7 — Reflex and Orthostatic Syncope

Vasovagal or reflex syncope often follows prolonged standing, pain, emotional stress, heat, or a situational trigger such as coughing, swallowing, urination, or defecation. Many patients have a prodrome of warmth, nausea, diaphoresis, lightheadedness, tunnel vision, or gray-out. Orthostatic syncope follows impaired compensatory blood-pressure response after standing and can be related to volume depletion, autonomic dysfunction, medications, or prolonged bed rest.

These patterns can be less dangerous in a patient with a normal initial evaluation, but they are not diagnoses of exclusion by age alone. Recurrent falls, injury, severe orthostatic symptoms, medication complexity, anemia, cardiac disease, or inability to maintain hydration can change management and disposition. Teach patients who have a recognized prodrome to sit or lie down safely and seek care when symptoms differ from their established pattern.

Part 8 — Cardiac Syncope: The Cannot-Miss Category

Syncope during exertion or while supine, sudden collapse with little or no prodrome, preceding palpitations, abnormal ECG, known structural heart disease, heart failure, prior arrhythmia, family history of premature sudden death, or concerning cardiac examination increases concern for arrhythmic or structural cardiac disease. Cardiac syncope can carry risk of sudden death and may require emergency or hospital-based evaluation, ambulatory rhythm monitoring, echocardiography, stress testing, or electrophysiology consultation based on the presentation.

Do not reassure solely because the patient is young, the episode was brief, or a single office ECG is normal. Conversely, not every syncopal event in an older adult is cardiac. Risk stratification integrates the event characteristics, ECG, cardiac history, injuries, vital signs, and current medical condition.

Part 9 — Medication and Metabolic Contributors

Medication review is an intervention, not a checkbox. Dizziness or syncope can arise from cumulative blood-pressure lowering, diuresis, sedatives, anticholinergic burden, alcohol, hypoglycemia-inducing therapy, or drug interactions. Make one medication change at a time when clinically safe, monitor blood pressure and symptoms, and coordinate with prescribers rather than stopping critical therapy abruptly.

Glucose measurement may be appropriate when hypoglycemia is possible, but an abnormal glucose result should be interpreted with the history. Anemia, infection, dehydration, electrolyte disorders, and pregnancy can also contribute. Target testing to the syndrome rather than ordering a generic dizziness panel.

Part 10 — FNP Case: Position-Triggered Vertigo

A 44-year-old reports seconds of spinning when rolling in bed or looking up, with normal gait between episodes and no weakness, diplopia, speech change, or new headache. The timing and trigger pattern support BPPV. The FNP confirms that the presentation is compatible, performs or refers for an appropriate maneuver within training, provides fall precautions, and gives return instructions for persistent, changed, or neurologic symptoms.

Part 11 — FNP Case: The Dizzy Patient Who Cannot Walk

A 69-year-old with diabetes and atrial fibrillation develops sudden vertigo, vomiting, double vision, and marked inability to stand without support. Calling this peripheral vertigo based on nausea would be unsafe. The neurologic symptoms, gait inability, and vascular risk demand emergency stroke-capable evaluation.

Part 12 — FNP Case: Syncope During Exercise

A 56-year-old loses consciousness while running, reports no warning symptoms, and has a family history of sudden death. This is not a routine vasovagal story. The FNP prioritizes ECG, emergency or urgent cardiac evaluation based on current status, and direct communication of exertional onset, absent prodrome, family history, medications, and exam findings.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Name the syndrome: vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium, nonspecific dizziness, true syncope, or a mimic.
  2. Use timing and triggers: brief triggered, episodic spontaneous, or continuous acute symptoms change the differential.
  3. Screen danger: focal neurologic signs, severe gait instability, double vision, new hearing or vision symptoms, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, exertional or supine syncope, abnormal vitals, or injury.
  4. Evaluate syncope deliberately: history, examination, orthostatic assessment when appropriate, ECG, medication review, and targeted tests.
  5. Choose disposition: emergency care for possible stroke, cardiac syncope, ongoing instability, serious injury, or dangerous secondary causes; close follow-up only after a low-risk evaluation and clear safety net.

Take-Home Summary

Dizziness is not one diagnosis, and syncope is not automatically benign. A time-and-trigger history plus focused neurologic, cardiovascular, gait, orthostatic, and medication assessment often clarifies the next step. FNP safety depends on identifying the patient with posterior stroke symptoms or cardiac syncope before pursuing a benign vestibular or vasovagal explanation. Clear return precautions and direct referral are part of treatment.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace individualized diagnosis, vestibular or neurologic examination training, current medication guidance, local stroke and emergency pathways, cardiology consultation, or emergency evaluation when red flags are present.
